analysis.one_liner: Bans high-commission investment plans and requires disclosures for insurance sold to troops on base.
analysis.headline: A bill to ban 50%-commission investment plans and require written disclosures before insurance sales on military bases died in the House Financial Services Committee without a hearing or vote.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would have outlawed "periodic payment plan certificates" — investments the bill's findings say carried a typical 50% commission on first-year contributions, versus under 6% for ordinary mutual funds — and required written, plain-language disclosures before anyone could sell life insurance in person to a service member on a military base. It also would have created a Pentagon registry of agents barred from bases, required insurers to report disciplined agents to state regulators, and directed the SEC to report on sales practices on installations and any refunds. It never moved past its referral to committee.
analysis.who_benefits: Military service members and their families, who were the target of high-cost investment and life insurance sales on bases; the bill's own findings state that some products offered to troops were "completely inappropriate for most military personnel" [S3]. Consumers generally also gain from the ban on the 50%-commission certificates and from toll-free access to broker and adviser disciplinary records [S2].

how_it_helps.text: Bans the sale of periodic payment plan certificates — the bill's findings note a 50% sales commission was typically charged against the first year of contributions, versus under 6% for other securities products, and that the product had largely vanished from the civilian market since the 1980s because of its cost [S3].

Requires written, plain-language disclosures before in-person life insurance sales to troops on military installations, including notice that subsidized federal life insurance may be available and that the government has not endorsed the product; agents who intentionally skip the disclosure could be barred from selling to federal employees on federal land [S3].

Orders the Defense Department to create and publish a registry of insurance and securities sellers who have been barred or banned from military installations, and requires insurers to report disciplinary actions against agents who sell on bases to state insurance commissioners [S3].

Clarifies that state insurance laws apply on military installations, closing a jurisdictional gap for sales on federal land, and directs states to work with the Pentagon on uniform anti-predatory-sales standards [S3].

Requires broker-dealer regulators to run toll-free lines and accessible processes so individual investors can check registration and disciplinary records of brokers and investment advisers, and directs the SEC to report on sales practices on military installations over five years and on refunds to service members [S2].

analysis.who_pays: Financial services firms that sold contractual plans and high-premium life insurance on military installations: fund companies and their underwriters lose the certificate business outright, and insurers and agents face disclosure duties, disciplinary reporting, and possible bans from federal facilities. Regulators and the Pentagon bear the administrative cost of new reporting systems and the barred-person registry [S3].
analysis.who_pays_short: Insurance and investment sellers on military bases

drawbacks.text: Much of the bill is hortatory: the uniform state standards (Section 7), the NAIC study of insurance product quality (Section 9), and the proposals to expand federal life insurance and improve the Thrift Savings Plan (Section 12) are framed as a 'sense of the Congress' with no enforcement mechanism [S3].

For life insurance, the bill leans on disclosure rather than prohibition — a service member could still be sold the same front-loaded, low-benefit policy after signing a written notice, so the protection depends on the buyer reading and understanding it [S3].

Several protections are delayed or enforcement-light: insurers' disciplinary reporting requirement only takes effect two years after enactment, and compliance is policed by state regulators and federal agencies, with no private right of action for service members to sue over violations [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The core benefits are real: an outright ban on a product whose 50% commission the bill itself documents, plus a registry of barred agents and mandatory disclosures on base. But the bill is better than many consumer bills and still modest in design — its insurance reforms mostly require disclosure rather than banning the products, its most ambitious ideas (uniform state standards, better federal life insurance and TSP benefits) are non-binding, and key reporting duties phase in over two years. An honest supporter would call it a solid floor-scraping fix, not a comprehensive overhaul, and the cost falls on the firms profiting from the sales practices the bill describes.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to the House Financial Services Committee the day it was introduced and never got a hearing, a vote, or any further action before that Congress ended.

narrative.text: Rahm Emanuel introduced the Military Personnel Financial Services Protection Act on February 1, 2005, with Chet Edwards as an original cosponsor; the bill was referred the same day to the House Committee on Financial Services [S5].
Seven Democrats cosponsored the bill; no Republican cosponsor appears on the record [S4].
The committee took no further action — no hearing, markup, or floor vote appears in the action history — and the bill died when the 109th Congress ended on January 3, 2007 [S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: The companies and agents selling high-commission investment certificates and front-loaded life insurance on military bases were better off: with the bill dead, they kept selling without the ban, the disclosures, the disciplinary reporting, or the Pentagon's barred-agent registry.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Firms selling high-cost products on bases

for.name: Rep. Rahm Emanuel
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and shepherded its referral to the Financial Services Committee

for.name: Rep. Chet Edwards
for.what_they_did: Joined as an original cosponsor at introduction

against.name: House Financial Services Committee (Chair Michael Oxley)
against.what_they_did: Never scheduled a hearing or markup, leaving the bill to die at the end of the Congress

sides.party_line_note: The sponsor and all seven cosponsors were Democrats and no vote was ever taken, so no partisan split on the bill itself was ever recorded.

industries.note: The bill bans issuance and sale of periodic payment plan certificates outright, ending a product line whose typical 50% first-year commission far exceeded the under-6% charged on ordinary mutual funds. Its civilian market had already largely collapsed since the 1980s; the military market was what remained [S3].

industries.industry: Life insurers and agents selling on military installations
industries.note: In-person sales to troops would require written disclosures noting federal subsidized life insurance exists, insurers would have to report disciplined agents to state regulators, and firms that intentionally skip disclosures could be barred from selling on federal land. The bill's findings call some of the products sold to troops 'completely inappropriate for most military personnel' [S3].

Firms lose the certificate business, and broker-dealers must report on their base sales practices and refunds to the SEC; in exchange, the bill formalizes industry-funded systems — toll-free lines and filing depositories — that give investors access to disciplinary records, with costs charged to non-individual inquirers [S3].
